Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- The failing test shortTextFilesAreNoTARs expects ArchiveStreamFactory.createArchiveInputStream(InputStream) to throw an ArchiveException with a “No Archiver found …” message when given a short plain-text InputStream.
- In ArchiveStreamFactory.createArchiveInputStream(InputStream), detection proceeds by reading signatures of increasing size:
  - Reads 12 bytes and checks Zip/Jar/Ar/Cpio signatures (all fail for plain text).
  - Reads 32 bytes and checks Dump signature (fails).
  - Reads 512 bytes into tarheader, then:
    - Calls TarArchiveInputStream.matches(tarheader, signatureLength). For short text, signatureLength < required tar offsets, so matches returns false (correctly not recognizing TAR at this stage).
- The bug is introduced by the COMPRESS-117 “improve auto-recognition” fallback immediately after the tar signature check:
  - Code creates a new TarArchiveInputStream over new ByteArrayInputStream(tarheader) and calls getNextEntry(). If this call does not throw, it assumes the input is a TAR and returns new TarArchiveInputStream(in).
  - Problem: tarheader is a 512-byte array that contains the few bytes read from the input followed by zero padding. For short text (< 100 bytes), those bytes land entirely in the TAR “name” field (100 bytes long) while all remaining fields (including size, checksum, magic, version) are zeros.
  - TarArchiveInputStream.getNextEntry() does not validate magic/version and only treats a block as EOF if all 512 bytes are zero. Since the first bytes are non-zero (the text), getRecord returns a “header” and new TarArchiveEntry(headerBuf) is constructed without throwing. As a result, getNextEntry() returns normally even though the data is not a valid TAR header.
  - The fallback therefore wrongly concludes “it’s a TAR” and returns a TarArchiveInputStream for the original InputStream.
- Why “<= 100 bytes” is special: 100 bytes is the TAR header’s name field length. If the input text fits entirely within those 100 bytes, the rest of the header remains zero-padded, which TarArchiveEntry tolerates, so no exception is thrown. For longer text, non-zero bytes spill into numeric fields (size, checksum, etc.), which are more likely to cause parsing issues and exceptions, so the false positive is less likely.
- Consequence in the test: The plain text (well under 100 bytes) passes the permissive fallback; createArchiveInputStream returns a TarArchiveInputStream instead of throwing, and the test fails with “created an input stream for a non-archive”.

Root cause:
- The COMPRESS-117 fallback in ArchiveStreamFactory.createArchiveInputStream(InputStream) uses the absence of an exception from TarArchiveInputStream.getNextEntry() as a proxy for “this is a TAR,” but TarArchiveInputStream does not perform strict header validation at that point. Combined with zero-padding the 512-byte tarheader buffer, this yields false positives for short text files.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
